title: Has Trend Following Changed Forever- - Systematic Investor - Ep.408

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Has Trend Following Changed Forever- - Systematic Investor - Ep.408.docx

speakers: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged, CTA background)
summary: Systematic Investor ep. 408: Niels and Alan review H1 2026 CTA performance, the new Fed chair's end of forward guidance, two pro-trend papers (Aspect, Systematica), and the CFM paper attributing the decline of short-term trend following to volatility-adjusted tick size and microstructure. Main conclusion: fast trend works only in large-tick markets; other explanations (pod shops, post-2009 regime, execution algos) are debated.

completeness_estimate: 0.93 - first reader was thorough (77 claims); misses are minor: early-July energy reversals, manager dispersion vs index, bond/equity YTD numbers, a volatility rationale for guidance, hidden small-tick liquidity, retail oil ETF risk.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they saw great uh complimentarity between um value and and momentum
claims.claim: Early quant investors (Grantham's earlier firm) combined momentum/trend with value because the two are complementary, so the combination diversifies better than either alone.
claims.testable: partly - factor combination testable, anecdote only

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they spent you know 10 years tinkering with it trying to enhance it you know all brought in modifications all that they felt were valid and made sense and they couldn't improve it.
claims.claim: Beyond a certain level a working quant model is very hard to improve by adding enhancements, so ten years of tinkering added nothing.
claims.conditions: applies once a model captures the core effect
claims.testable: partly - can be tested via out-of-sample enhancement trials

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: as soon as they implemented it, it didn't work for six years or something and then they had to park it
claims.claim: A factor (the neglect factor, stocks without analyst coverage) with strong research results failed for years after live implementation, showing in-sample research often does not survive going live.
claims.testable: yes - in-sample vs live degradation measurable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we haven't really made any changes to the model because we don't think there's anything wrong with the model. It's just that at the moment there's just not a lot of trends.
claims.claim: Trend followers should not change a sound model during a poor period (the CTA winter), because poor results reflect an absence of trends rather than a model flaw.
claims.testable: partly - hard to separate model flaw from regime

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I guess it's it's also in a sense a sign of of the fact that there are lots of people who are struggling who simply can't pay normal prices.
claims.claim: US retailers selling smaller pack sizes signals stretched consumers who cannot pay normal prices.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the CME group is going to now offer a different new contract for oil and is only going to be based on 10 barrels instead of a,000 barrels
claims.claim: CME is launching a 10-barrel oil contract (vs 1,000) to attract retail money, a smaller contract size.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I'm thinking specifically about the craze around silver last year. A lot of people got got in quite late.
claims.claim: Retail inflows into a market tend to arrive late near highs (silver last year), so retail access expansion can mean losses for unprepared participants.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it certainly helps if you're a you know even if you're kind of a semi-pro and you're trying to run a small small portfolio it's definitely helpful from that perspective
claims.claim: Micro futures contracts make it practical for small systematic portfolios to trade diversified futures.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer yesterday closed at 50, which is a decent strong number.
claims.claim: The trend barometer (a trend-strength gauge) at 50 shows a decent strong trend environment for CTAs in H1 2026.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: people who did non-trend stuff inside their strategies probably did a little bit better
claims.claim: In H1 2026, CTAs that included non-trend strategies did somewhat better than pure trend followers.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: people who traded alternative markets uh which be obviously became very popular a few years ago, they struggled
claims.claim: CTAs trading alternative (non-traditional) markets struggled in H1 2026, with few exceptions.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think we had a lot of reversals in commodities in Junely uh linked to um the Middle East.
claims.claim: June 2026 saw many commodity reversals tied to Middle East news (metals, soybean oil), hurting trend managers, followed by rebounds in July.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it see it still feels like a good environment. Plenty of directional movement, plenty of uh volatility.
claims.claim: Directional movement and volatility make 2026 a good environment for trend following, better than average year to date.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we know historically because uh we can see the data that actually 2022 turned out to be a really great year for CTAs.
claims.claim: The 2026 commodity surge and super-cycle talk resembles 2022 (Ukraine), when commodities collapsed after a spike yet CTAs had a great year, so trend followers need not predict.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the market was able to withstand this for for a matter of weeks or couple of months.
claims.claim: Predicted oil-supply shock from the Strait of Hormuz disruption did not cause a price spike because China tapped reserves and flows were rerouted, so consensus pessimism was too severe.
claims.indicator: oil price, Strait of Hormuz disruption
claims.conditions: if disruption persists the shock could still occur

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: copper is is a good reflection of the AI uh theme
claims.claim: Copper demand reflects the AI/data-center capex theme, a demand-side story that supports the commodity trend independent of supply disruptions.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that's the beauty of what we do, Alan, is we don't actually have to predict um what what's going to happen
claims.claim: Systematic trend followers do not need forecasts; they follow trends as they develop.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Stocken CTA index down 46 basis points in July, still up 8.9% for the year.
claims.claim: As of 7 July 2026 the Stocken CTA index was down 46 bp in July and up 8.9% YTD, with the trend index up 8.5% and short-term traders up 4.65%, so slower trend outperformed short-term traders.
claims.indicator: CTA index, trend index, short-term traders index

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: he's not a fan of forward guidance. He he he doesn't like it. He he thinks it can kind of put the Fed in a bit of a box.
claims.claim: New Fed chair Warsh dislikes forward guidance and wants markets to infer policy from data, shifting the Fed toward less communication.
claims.testable: partly - regime change measurable by vol

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: very often you would get a move in bond yields or whatever and reflecting the fundamentals and the Fed was would effectively validate that.
claims.claim: In the Greenspan era the Fed often validated moves markets had already priced from the data, which is the model Warsh wants to return to.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: cocoa that's keeps sort of uh surging now suddenly after it was in a in a big downtrend for a while
claims.claim: Cocoa surged in early July 2026 after a long downtrend, a trend-reversal move.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the whole point about communications was try and guide long-term rates when they couldn't really um influence them.
claims.claim: Forward guidance was introduced (Bernanke, 2004) to steer long-term rates before QE, because the Fed controlled only short rates.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: 68% of the variance in the 5-year Treasury yield after a Fed me meeting um that was attributable to um to to the um to the statement
claims.claim: A study found 68% of 5-year Treasury yield variance after Fed meetings came from the statement and only 12% from the rate decision, so markets are addicted to Fed communication.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: simplistically would suggest more volatility because there's going to be more uncertainty.
claims.claim: Less forward guidance should mean more uncertainty and more volatility around Fed policy.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the market kind of factors in a full tightening cycle straight away whereas if it's going to be more incremental it's going to take time for the market to infer the extent of a tightening cycle
claims.claim: Without Fed projections of the rate path, markets will price tightening cycles incrementally, producing slower information absorption and longer trends in rates.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you might see a bigger term premier on on bond markets as well because of this because of the uncertainty.
claims.claim: Less Fed guidance raises uncertainty and therefore the bond term premium.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: When you get a productivity shock, there's a supply element and a demand element. We're experiencing the demand element now.
claims.claim: The AI productivity shock raises prices now via demand (chips, memory, electricity) while its disinflationary supply effect arrives later, creating a dilemma like Greenspan's 1990s.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: raise rates now to kind of cool the the the demand from from the AI capics boom even though you think it's going to be disinflationary down the line
claims.claim: Warsh faces the choice of tightening against AI-driven demand despite expected future disinflation; Alan doubts he is as hawkish as the market inferred.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Apple raising their prices 20 25% in a day
claims.claim: Large Apple price increases will show up in inflation data as AI hardware cost pass-through.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I'm actually quite interested in what are they going to change in terms of the economic data they want to publish.
claims.claim: Changes to published economic data would break models built on those series, so data-definition risk matters for systematic models.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the last 25 years were effectively an anomaly in terms of kind of abundant energy and the peace dividend from globalization
claims.claim: Aspect argues the last 25 years were an anomaly of cheap energy and globalization peace dividend, now ending with structural breaks that favor trend following.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: bonds are are less diver less reliable uh diversifiers for equities
claims.claim: Bonds are now less reliable diversifiers for equities, while gold demand from central banks and the dollar's store-of-value role are reassessed.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: a strategy that is adaptive for, you know, for for for regime change
claims.claim: Trend following is an adaptive diversifier for regime change and a managed way to gain commodity exposure.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it's not just an an oil shock that that that we need to think about. There are other kinds of shocks
claims.claim: Supply shocks in copper, food or other commodities can also hurt bonds and equities, so oil is not the only relevant scenario.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we could have a fiscal shock or a fiscal uh problem in the bond market that could impact bonds and equities
claims.claim: Fiscal problems or large dollar moves could hit traditional assets, so portfolios need diversifiers across currencies and rates.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: recognizing the I suppose the the the failings and the drawbacks of strategic asset allocation
claims.claim: Systematica argues the total portfolio approach beats strategic asset allocation because bonds no longer diversify equity risk.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: many other hedge fund strategies you know are take give you a lot of equity risk and as does private equities.
claims.claim: Many hedge fund strategies and private equity carry hidden equity beta, so true diversifiers are scarce.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the likes of equity market neutral is is a good diversifier but it's it's unlikely to give you that convexity.
claims.claim: Equity market neutral diversifies but lacks convexity, so trend following is complementary through dynamic risk management.
claims.indicator: convexity of trend vs equity market neutral

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: not so much which assets you should have in your portfolio but more about the kind of the behavior you should own
claims.claim: Portfolio construction should target behavioral exposures (e.g., trend, carry) rather than asset-class lists.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's much more about kind of the impact that uh say a strategy has on the total uh portfolio, not so much about how it does relative to a few other similar type strategies.
claims.claim: Under the total portfolio approach, strategies are judged by their contribution to the whole portfolio rather than versus peers.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: short-term trading doesn't seem to work uh as well anymore
claims.claim: Short-term trend following has deteriorated, shown by weak short-term managers and by slower parameter settings doing better in own models.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: parameter settings have probably become longer slower systems have done well
claims.claim: The CFM paper formalizes what practitioners saw: slower trend systems have outperformed fast ones.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we used to hear the industry has got too big you know so that was the source of the degradation in returns but actually that's not consist consistent with the evidence
claims.claim: Crowding by industry size does not explain weaker fast trend returns because CTA AUM stagnated while futures liquidity grew, so the CTA footprint shrank.
claims.indicator: CTA AUM vs futures market liquidity

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the electronification of futures interest rate futures markets has come along and has had no impact on the the profitability
claims.claim: Electronification does not explain the decline since rate futures electronified without a profitability loss.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the volatility adjusted tick size that that's a key variable for how uh conducive a market is for fast trend following.
claims.claim: The CFM paper finds volatility-adjusted tick size is the key variable for whether a market suits fast trend following: large-tick markets (bonds, rates, some commodities) work, small-tick ones (currencies) do not.
claims.direction: fast trend in large-tick markets only
claims.conditions: small-tick markets such as FX and equities fail

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: what did the bank do then? Well the bank then they called up all of the other banks and they bought again.
claims.claim: Historically dealers laid off a CTA's large order by trading with other dealers, a chain of buying that created momentum in the price and so profited fast trend followers.
claims.conditions: when banks warehouse risk and quote size
claims.testable: partly - mechanism inferred, not directly measured

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: momentum effect that comes from the actual trading was is a key part of what drives trend following returns
claims.claim: The paper's thesis: part of fast trend returns comes from the price momentum generated by trend followers' own order flow, beside behavioral causes.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: behavioral factors like um you know the speed of adjustment for different participants in the market and underreaction initially and then overreaction later
claims.claim: The standard behavioral explanation for trend following is heterogeneous adjustment speeds with initial underreaction then overreaction.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: something changed around 2010 where you had a lot more high frequency traders um and the banks uh basically took a step back from from warehousing risk like that.
claims.claim: After 2010 high-frequency traders rose and banks stopped warehousing risk, so large orders could no longer be executed cheaply and fast trend lost momentum from execution.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: that creates that creates maybe arguably less momentum itself.
claims.claim: If CTAs all trade passively and slowly, their orders would create less momentum themselves, so changed CTA behavior may contribute.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: in the large tick size contracts fast trend following does seem to to to work.
claims.claim: Fast trend still works in large-tick contracts (bonds, rates, some commodities); the weakness is concentrated in equities and currencies, so the headline overstates the decline.
claims.indicator: fast trend returns by tick size
claims.direction: long fast trend in large-tick markets

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: there used to be a lot more liquidity available for trend followers. So if you were looking to to buy, there was plenty of liquidity there.
claims.claim: Order-book data show less liquidity available to trend followers since 2010 as providers withdrew.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: markets seem to be much more uh mean reverting at shortterm time horizons
claims.claim: Counter-trend trades have become more dominant, so after breaks there is a reversal rather than follow-through, making markets more mean reverting at short horizons.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's it stopped working basically between 2010 and 2020. But since 2020 its performance has has kind of improved again
claims.claim: Figure 10 shows fast trend working poorly between 2010 and 2020 but improving since, so it may be a decade-long drought rather than a permanent break.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you look at the large tick, uh there's no evidence of a CTA winter there at all for any time frame.
claims.claim: In large-tick markets there is no CTA winter at any lookback, and fast trend did better over 1995 onward, implying the winter is concentrated in small-tick markets.

correction.issue: Omits that Alan also says slow trend was quite challenged from about 2008 in large-tick markets before picking up recently; the 'no CTA winter at any time frame' remark sits beside this contradicting caveat.
correction.fix: In large-tick markets fast trend did better over the full period since 1995; slow trend was challenged from about 2008 and recovered more recently, though Alan also says the large-tick chart shows no clear CTA winter for any time frame.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Does it mean that CTAs have to penalize uh you know the small tick contracts and be cognizant of this effect if you're going to trade faster?
claims.claim: Practical implication: CTAs trading fast should reduce weight or penalize small-tick contracts, as they already penalize illiquid contracts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: yes it's has to mean as good but still from a crisis alpha perspective it can be can can still have um can still have a merit
claims.claim: Even if fast trend returns degraded, it can still add convexity, skew and crisis alpha (Man papers).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: short-term time frames on a classical trend following model has not been profitable whatsoever for the past 15 years.
claims.claim: Niels's internal tests: short-term timeframes of a classical trend model have not been profitable for 15 years, with a break around 2009.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we could run our own simulations um based on markets with small tick size for the contracts and and markets with large tick size um and and keeping the model consistent.
claims.claim: Managers can replicate the CFM result by running one model separately on small-tick and large-tick contracts.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the environment change after 09? Maybe because we had a big global financial crisis that ended in 09 and we know that uh central banks got much more involved and and so on and so forth.
claims.claim: Post-2009 central bank involvement and changed participants may explain fast trend's decline instead of tick size.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: banks not being allowed to trade a lot on their own book and actually you had to outsource it
claims.claim: Post-2009 rules on bank proprietary trading changed market participants and liquidity provision.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you get a call on a Friday afternoon uh that you need to cut your risk by 50%
claims.claim: Multi-manager pod shops cut risk quickly on small drawdowns, and their AUM growth likely changed short-term microstructure toward mean reversion.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the other thing we've had in equities has been you know zero TD DTEES more volatility selling
claims.claim: Equity microstructure changed through 0DTE options, volatility selling and structured products, which may hurt fast equity trend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you have to trade a lot more contracts. That means your commission costs go up significantly.
claims.claim: Small contracts have unchanged per-contract fees, so same exposure costs more; a backtest must reflect that cost.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they actually find trends are better in low low volatility
claims.claim: Fast trend does better in low volatility, and what has vanished is the ability to profit from large one-day directional moves.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: what's been eliminated specifically is trend followers ability to profit from large directional kind of one day moves.
claims.claim: Trend followers can no longer profit from large one-day moves since execution into them is costly.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: But then they did look at liquidity as a variable itself and and that didn't explain it cross-sectionally.
claims.claim: Liquidity alone did not explain the cross-section; contract characteristics plus liquidity together do.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the question is not how many people do you trade with. To me it's more like how big is the size that you're trading um visav the total size of the market.
claims.claim: Momentum from execution depends on order size relative to the market, not on the number of counterparties.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: most of the trend followers say but we don't do much short-term because the evidence shows it's been deteriorating for for for a long time
claims.claim: Most trend followers already avoid short-term, so degradation of fast trend is unlikely to be the main driver of CTA returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you used to have more momentum type uh participants now you may have more mean reverting type managers like uh high frequency
claims.claim: Short-horizon participants have shifted from momentum types to mean-reverting high-frequency traders.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you're kind of going to miss the big kind of breakout moves because you're wait you're you're you're passive
claims.claim: Passive execution misses breakouts; aggressive execution is costly.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some people just go straight from from the from the signal to the to the exchange um and they incorporate some kind of algo
claims.claim: Execution now goes from signal to exchange via algorithms that behave differently from human traders, which may contribute to changes in short-term dynamics.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the last couple of days we've had some reversals now again given the renewed um bombing campaigns uh happening in the Middle East
claims.claim: Early July 2026 was quiet to soft for CTAs, with renewed Middle East bombing campaigns causing direction reversals, especially in energy markets, which hurt trend positions.
claims.direction: energy trends reverse; CTA returns soft
claims.testable: partly - CTA returns around Middle East event dates

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you had the oil ETF can't remember exactly what it was called but you know you know and that ran into challenges obviously when when oil went the one that went negative
claims.claim: Retail already speculates on oil through ETFs and spread betting even without futures access, and the retail oil ETF ran into trouble when front oil futures went negative, showing structural product risk for retail commodity vehicles.
claims.indicator: retail oil ETF (negative oil price episode)
claims.testable: partly - ETF tracking vs futures in April 2020

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I thought they were generally a bit more negative than the index. I think the index was down less than a couple of percent
claims.claim: In June 2026 the individual CTA managers Alan monitors did worse than the CTA index (index down under 2%), with more negatives than positives, i.e. high manager dispersion around the index.
claims.indicator: CTA index vs individual manager returns
claims.testable: yes - manager return dispersion vs index

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: bond index down 56 basis points u for the month uh up only a quarter% or so um this year
claims.claim: As of 7 July 2026 the US aggregate bond index was up only about 0.25% YTD while the S&P 500 total return was up about 10% and MSCI World 9.65%, so CTA indices (8.5-8.9%) roughly matched equities while bonds gave almost nothing.
claims.indicator: US Aggregate bond index, S&P 500 TR, MSCI World YTD
claims.direction: bonds flat, equities and CTAs up

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: There's also a sense that you know you know more shocks created more volatility which was seen to be a a bad thing.
claims.claim: A second rationale for Fed transparency was that policy surprises create market volatility, so forward guidance was meant to reduce shock-driven volatility; after the GFC, committing to low rates for long became a core unconventional tool.
claims.testable: partly - yield volatility around FOMC by communication regime

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the liquidity is there but it's not necessarily apparent right that it at at the at the kind of represented bid offer
claims.claim: In small-tick markets liquidity exists but is not displayed at the quoted bid/offer, whereas before high-frequency trading large size was visible at the touch, so a trend follower could no longer see and take big size at one price.
claims.indicator: displayed top-of-book depth vs tick size
claims.testable: yes - order book depth by volatility-adjusted tick size
